subject: Art & Design
source: National Curriculum (Art and Design). Drive Art & Design folder reviewed (Elements of Art deck, KS3 files) and the school's 'Art - Y9' lesson plan example used for format and the Y9 Zentangle topic. | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 3 to 7, v3): Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7 (still life, watercolour and mark making); objects only, no people

lessons.title: The elements of art: line, shape, form, colour, tone, texture, space
objectives: Name and define the seven elements of art
Create a sampler using each element

keywords.def: a mark that connects two points and shows direction
a three-dimensional shape with height, width and depth
how light or dark something is
how a surface looks or feels
the area around and between things in an artwork

starter: Bismillah. Name the three primary colours.

teach.heading: Seven elements
teach.note: Show a simple Islamic tile and ask pupils to find line, shape and colour. Pupils need pencil, paper, black pen, colours. Drive deck 'Elements of Art' is a good support.

teach.heading: Line, shape and form
bullets: A circle is a shape; a sphere is a form
teach.note: Draw a circle and a sphere with shading. Misconception: shape and form are the same.

teach.heading: Colour, tone and texture
teach.note: Tone can be done in a pencil. Ask pupils to describe a texture near them.

teach.heading: Space
teach.note: Draw a vase and ask what is the space around it.

teach.heading: Making a sampler
teach.note: Allow 15 minutes. Circulate and pose questions: Which element is your strongest?

practice: What is the difference between shape and form?
Is a rough surface a texture or a tone?
independent: Name the elements in a simple pattern you describe.
Draw a 3D cube and say what makes it a form.
exit: Complete the seven-box sampler with labels.
Add a sentence saying which element you found hardest.
homework: Give one example of negative space.
lessons.send: Find an object at home and describe it using at least four elements.

lessons.title: Tone and form: drawing a sphere
objectives: Use hatching and blending to show form
Draw a sphere with a light source and cast shadow
Evaluate your drawing using the success criteria

keywords.def: where the light comes from
the shadow an object makes on the surface beside it
the brightest part of an object
to smooth tones into each other

starter: Define tone in your own words.

teach.heading: From circle to sphere
teach.note: Pupils need HB or 2B pencil, paper, a tissue or finger for blending. Show a ball under a lamp.

teach.heading: Five tones
teach.note: Label each on a board sketch. Misconception: the darkest part is the edge; the core shadow is inside it.

teach.heading: Drawing step by step
teach.note: Slow, step-by-step demo. Check where the cast shadow goes (opposite the light).

teach.heading: Blending
teach.note: Give pupils two minutes to blend. Remind them that patience improves smoothness.

teach.heading: Self-assessment
bullets: Is the shadow opposite the light?
teach.note: Pupils check against the three criteria and write one target.

practice: Where does a shadow fall if light is on the left?
What is the brightest part called?
independent: Shade a flat circle into a sphere.
exit: Draw a sphere with a cast shadow and at least five tones.
Draw a second sphere with the light from the opposite side.
homework: What are the five tones on a sphere?
How does tone help show form?
lessons.send: Draw a round fruit or ball from life using five tones.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Still life: observation, watercolour and mark making
lessons.title: Still life: looking closely at everyday objects
lessons.bigQuestion: Why might an artist spend weeks painting a bowl of apples instead of a famous building?
objectives: To understand how artists choose and arrange everyday objects to make a still life composition
successCriteria: All: set up a still life of three household objects
Most: use overlap and different heights to make the arrangement interesting
Some: explain the colour choices in an arrangement using the colour wheel
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: how light and shadow show the form of an object
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for everyday blessings, noticed through careful looking

keywords.def: art of objects that do not move, such as fruit, bottles and jugs
how things are arranged in a picture
one object partly in front of another
colours opposite on the colour wheel, such as red and green

hook.text: Why might an artist spend weeks painting a bowl of apples instead of a famous building?
hook.a: Ordinary objects teach looking: shape, light, colour and texture, without distraction.

islamicLink.text: Muslim artists have long focused on objects, plants, geometry and calligraphy rather than people. Allah says He 'perfected everything He created' (as-Sajdah 32:7): looking closely at an apple or a jug trains us to notice and be grateful for the detail in ordinary things.

starter.q: Which are the three primary colours (paint)?
Mix yellow and blue. What do you get?
What is the complementary colour of orange?
Name two of the seven elements of art.
starter.a: Any two of line, shape, form, colour, value, texture, space.

teach.heading: What is still life?
bullets: An old tradition in many cultures
teach.note: Show the photos of arranged objects. Still life lets us study shape, light and texture slowly.

teach.heading: Making a good arrangement
teach.note: Model live on camera with a mug, an orange and a bottle under a desk lamp.

right.title: Strong arrangement
points: Light from one side, clear shadows

teach.heading: Colour wheel recap
teach.note: An orange beside a blue mug makes both look brighter.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which arrangement is most interesting to draw?
options: Three objects in a straight row
Three objects grouped with overlap and different heights
check.why: Overlap and varied heights create depth and rhythm; rows and identical objects look flat.

practice.q: Look at the photo of the arrangement. Which object is in front, and how do you know?
practice.a: The orange: it overlaps the bottom of the mug.
practice.model: Teacher points: the orange hides part of the mug, so it is closer to us. Overlap shows depth.

practice.q: Where is the light coming from in the photo?
practice.a: From the left: shadows fall to the right.

practice.q: Name a complementary pair you could use in your arrangement.
practice.a: For example: a red apple and a green cloth.

independent.q: Core: Set up your own still life of three household objects with overlap and side light. Photograph it and upload it to the portal.
independent.a: A photo with three objects, overlap, varied heights and side lighting.
independent.model: Teacher arranges, then moves the lamp to one side and talks about the shadows.

independent.q: Extend: Make three quick thumbnail sketches (2 minutes each) from three different viewpoints. Circle the best.
independent.a: Three thumbnails with the strongest composition chosen.

independent.q: Stretch: Write two sentences in the portal response box on why you chose your objects and colours. Start: 'I chose... because...'
independent.a: For example: I chose an orange and a blue mug because they are complementary and make each other stand out.

exit.q: A still life is a picture of... A) people B) objects that do not move C) moving animals
exit.a: B) objects that do not move

exit.q: Big question: why paint a bowl of apples? Give one reason.
exit.a: It trains careful looking at shape, light, colour and texture.

lessons.homework: Keep your still life set up (or photographed) for the next four lessons; draw one object from it in outline for 10 minutes.
lessons.send: SEND: a ready-made arrangement photo to use. EAL: overlap, arrange, light with gestures. Stretch: add a patterned cloth and plan its colours.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (Year 7 still life half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7
At home: three household objects (a mug, a fruit, a bottle), a desk lamp, sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, eraser
Colour wheel sheet (pupil PDF)
Teacher's live still life on camera (mug, orange, bottle, desk lamp)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Still life: observation, watercolour and mark making
lessons.title: Line and shape: drawing objects in outline
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does the top of a mug look like an oval, not a circle, when it is on the table in front of you?
objectives: To understand how accurate outlines come from looking at shapes, proportions and negative space
successCriteria: All: draw the outline of one object using light guide lines
Most: measure proportions with a pencil held at arm's length
Some: use negative space to check the outline of a group of objects
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: ratio and proportion (height to width)
lessons.smsc: Moral: patience and accuracy (itqan in doing a task well)

keywords.def: a mark that shows edges and direction
the line around the outside of a shape
the size of one part compared with another
the empty space around and between objects
the oval a circle makes when seen at an angle

hook.text: Why does the top of a mug look like an oval, not a circle, when it is on the table in front of you?
hook.a: We see the circle at an angle, so it becomes an ellipse.

starter.q: Name a complementary pair.
Why do artists overlap objects in a still life?
starter.a: To show depth (which is in front).

starter.q: How many objects make a good small still life?
starter.a: An odd number, such as three.

starter.q: Which of the seven elements is the path of a moving point?

teach.heading: Draw what you see
teach.note: Model the mug as a cylinder: two ellipses and two straight sides.

teach.heading: Measuring with a pencil
teach.note: Model: the bottle is 3 mugs tall.

model.problem: How tall is the bottle compared with the mug?
steps: Hold the pencil at arm's length
Line the tip with the top of the mug, thumb at the base
Move the same length up the bottle
It fits 2 and a half times
model.answer: The bottle is 2.5 times the mug's height

teach.heading: Ellipses and negative space
bullets: A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse
Both ends are rounded, never pointed
Draw the shapes of the gaps too
teach.note: Common error shown.

misconception.wrong: Draw the top of a cup as a flat line or a lemon shape with points
misconception.right: Draw a smooth ellipse with rounded ends; the base ellipse is a little rounder than the top

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: The empty space between a mug's handle and its side is called...
check.why: Negative space is the shape around and between objects; drawing it checks the outline.

practice.q: Draw a cylinder (mug shape) with two ellipses and two straight sides.
practice.a: Top ellipse, straight sides, rounded base ellipse.
practice.model: Teacher draws on the visualiser: light top ellipse, two vertical lines, base ellipse slightly rounder, then firms the visible edges.

practice.q: Measure: how many times does your mug's width fit into its height?
practice.a: Depends on the mug; for example about 1.2 times.

independent.q: Core: Draw your three-object still life in outline only, with light guide lines and measured proportions.
independent.a: A clear outline drawing with proportions checked and overlaps shown.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first object (the mug) from measurement to final line.

independent.q: Extend: Shade only the negative spaces lightly to check the shapes.
independent.a: The gaps between objects shaded, showing any errors.

independent.q: Stretch: Vary the line weight: darker lines for nearer edges, lighter for further.
independent.a: Clear difference in line weight giving depth.

exit.q: A circle seen at an angle becomes... A) a square B) an ellipse C) a triangle
exit.a: B) an ellipse

exit.q: Big question: why does the top of a mug look like an oval?
exit.a: We see the circle at an angle, so it becomes an ellipse.

lessons.homework: Draw five ellipses: a cup, a bowl, a jar lid, a plate and a roll of tape, all from life.
lessons.send: SEND: a traced outline sheet to check proportions. EAL: outline, measure, ellipse with diagrams. Stretch: draw the group from a high viewpoint.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (Year 7 still life half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7
At home: three household objects (a mug, a fruit, a bottle), a desk lamp, sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, eraser
Upload of the outline drawing to the portal (photo)

pictures.alt: A mug seen from the side

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Still life: observation, watercolour and mark making
lessons.title: Value: tone and shading
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a pencil, which only makes grey, make a drawing look round and solid?
objectives: To understand how a range of tones makes a flat outline look three-dimensional
successCriteria: All: make a tonal scale of five values from light to dark
Most: shade an object with a highlight, mid-tones, a core shadow and a cast shadow
Some: blend smoothly and keep the light direction consistent across the still life
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: light travels in straight lines and is blocked to make shadows
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on light and darkness in creation (al-An'am 6:1)

keywords.def: how light or dark a tone is
a shade of light or dark
the brightest spot where light hits
the shadow an object throws onto the surface
an object's three-dimensional shape

hook.text: How can a pencil, which only makes grey, make a drawing look round and solid?
hook.a: By changing tone from light to dark across the form, following the light.

starter.q: What is negative space?
starter.a: The space around and between objects.
options: The space around and between objects

starter.q: Why measure with a pencil at arm's length?
starter.a: To compare sizes and get proportions right.

starter.q: Which pencil is softer and darker, HB or 2B?
Name the element of art for light and dark.

teach.heading: A tonal scale
teach.note: Model a five-box scale: 1 paper white, 5 darkest.

teach.heading: Light on a form
bullets: Core shadow: darkest on the object
teach.note: Use the lamp on the orange to show each part.

teach.heading: Shading a sphere
bullets: Build dark away from the light
teach.note: Model on an orange.

model.problem: Shade an orange lit from the top left.
steps: Circle outline; mark light arrow top left
Leave a small highlight top left
Mid-tones in curved strokes
Darkest core shadow bottom right; cast shadow to the right
model.answer: A round form with tones following the light

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Light comes from the left. Where is the cast shadow?
check.why: Shadows fall on the side away from the light.

practice.a: Five boxes, evenly stepped from white to dark.
practice.model: Teacher shades boxes 5 then 1, then fills 3 halfway between, then 2 and 4.

practice.q: Shade a sphere with the light from the top right.
practice.a: Highlight top right, core and cast shadow bottom left.

independent.q: Core: Shade your still life outline with at least four tones and the same light direction for every object.
independent.a: Consistent light; highlight, mid-tone, core and cast shadow on each object.
independent.model: Teacher shades the mug's left side and cast shadow first.

independent.q: Extend: Show reflected light: a slightly lighter band at the edge of the shadow side.
independent.a: A visible lighter band inside the shadow edge.

independent.q: Stretch: Write in the portal response box how tone shows form. Start: 'Tone makes the orange look round because...'
independent.a: Tone makes the orange look round because the light changes gradually from the highlight to the core shadow, following its curved surface.

exit.q: The brightest spot on an object is the... A) cast shadow B) highlight C) core shadow
exit.a: B) highlight

exit.q: Big question: how does a grey pencil make something look solid?
exit.a: By changing tone gradually from light to dark following the light.

lessons.homework: Shade an egg (or a ball) lit by one lamp, showing all five parts of light on a form.
lessons.send: SEND: a printed tonal scale to copy. EAL: light, dark, shadow with picture labels. Stretch: use cross-hatching for the darkest tones.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (Year 7 still life half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7
At home: three household objects (a mug, a fruit, a bottle), a desk lamp, sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, eraser
Tonal scale worksheet (pupil PDF)

pictures.alt: A lit sphere showing highlight and shadow
An orange with a cast shadow

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Still life: observation, watercolour and mark making
lessons.title: Mark making with pen and pencil
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you draw something smooth, rough, shiny and soft using only a black pen?
objectives: To understand how different marks create tone and texture in a drawing
successCriteria: All: make six different marks (hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, scribble, contour lines, dashes)
Most: use marks to build tone from light to dark
Some: choose marks that match each object's texture
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: technical drawings use hatching to show cut surfaces
lessons.smsc: Cultural: pen and ink traditions, including the qalam in Arabic calligraphy

keywords.def: the lines, dots and patterns an artist makes
parallel lines to make tone
layers of crossing lines for darker tone
dots that build up tone
how a surface feels or looks as if it would feel

hook.text: Can you draw something smooth, rough, shiny and soft using only a black pen?
hook.a: Yes: different marks suggest different textures.

starter.q: Light is on the right. Where is the cast shadow?
Name the brightest part of a lit object.
How many steps were in our tonal scale?
Which pencil is darker: HB or 2B?

teach.heading: A library of marks
teach.note: Model each in a grid of six boxes with a fine black pen.

teach.heading: Marks build tone
teach.note: Cross-hatching: add a layer at a new angle for each step.

teach.heading: Model: tone with marks
teach.note: Model on a bottle.

model.problem: Shade a glass bottle using pen marks only.
steps: Leave highlights as white paper
Contour hatching for mid-tones, following the curve
Cross-hatch the darkest side
Stipple the cast shadow
model.answer: Tone and form from marks, no smudging

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Many crossing layers close together cover the most paper.

practice.q: Fill a grid of six boxes, one mark in each.
practice.a: Six labelled boxes: hatching, cross-hatching, stippling, scribble, contour lines, dashes.
practice.model: Teacher fills the hatching and cross-hatching boxes, naming each.

practice.q: Make a five-step tonal scale using only cross-hatching.

independent.q: Core: Redraw one object from your still life and give it tone using pen marks only.
independent.a: An object with three or more tones made by marks, highlight left white.
independent.model: Teacher starts the bottle from the model slide.

independent.q: Extend: Give each object in your still life a different mark that suits its texture.
independent.a: Marks match textures (for example stippling on the orange skin, smooth hatching on the glass).

independent.q: Stretch: Annotate your sheet: label three marks and say what texture each shows.
independent.a: Three labelled marks with textures named.

exit.q: Dots that build up tone are called... A) hatching B) stippling C) scribble
exit.a: B) stippling

exit.q: Big question: name one mark for a smooth surface and one for a rough surface.
exit.a: For example: even hatching (smooth), scribble or flicks (rough).

lessons.homework: Make a mark-making sampler of ten marks from textures you find at home (a towel, wood, a leaf).
lessons.send: SEND: a printed grid with mark examples. EAL: mark names with pictures. Stretch: an object drawn with stippling only.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (Year 7 still life half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7
At home: three household objects (a mug, a fruit, a bottle), a desk lamp, sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, eraser
Fine black pen (or biro)
Mark-making grid (pupil PDF)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Still life: observation, watercolour and mark making
lessons.title: Watercolour wash on the still life; evaluate
lessons.bigQuestion: Watercolour has no white paint. How do artists show the brightest highlights?
objectives: To understand how watercolour washes add colour while keeping the drawing's tone and light
successCriteria: All: paint a flat wash and a graded wash
Most: work light to dark, leaving the paper white for highlights
Some: evaluate the finished still life against the success criteria
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: dissolving and dilution: more water, paler colour
lessons.smsc: Social: kind, specific peer feedback (what went well, even better if)

keywords.def: transparent paint mixed with water
a thin, even layer of watercolour
a wash that changes from strong to pale
painting onto dry paper for sharp edges
judge strengths and next steps

hook.text: Watercolour has no white paint. How do artists show the brightest highlights?
hook.a: They leave the white paper unpainted.

starter.q: Which mark makes the darkest tone?
What is a highlight?
starter.a: The brightest spot where light hits.

starter.q: Name the complementary colour of purple.
What is negative space?
starter.a: The space around and between objects.

teach.heading: Watercolour basics
bullets: No white paint: keep the paper
teach.note: Kit: a cheap school watercolour set, a round brush, two water pots (clean and dirty), kitchen roll.

teach.heading: Flat and graded wash
teach.note: Model both washes.

steps: Mix a puddle of blue
Paint one stripe across the top
Add a little water, paint the next stripe overlapping
Repeat until almost clear
model.answer: A smooth wash from strong to pale

teach.heading: Light to dark
bullets: First layer pale everywhere except highlights
Add darker layers to the shadows
teach.note: Patience: wait for each layer to dry.

teach.heading: Evaluate
teach.note: Model one evaluation sentence for each.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: How do you make watercolour paler?
check.why: Watercolour is transparent: more water dilutes it. White paint makes it chalky and opaque.

practice.q: Paint a flat wash and a graded wash in two boxes.
practice.a: One even box; one fading from strong to pale.
practice.model: Teacher paints both on camera, talking about how much water is on the brush.

practice.q: Where on your orange will you leave white paper?
practice.a: The highlight, on the side facing the light.

independent.q: Core: Add a watercolour wash to your shaded still life: pale first, highlights left white, darker layers in the shadows.
independent.a: A still life with transparent colour, highlights kept, shadows darker.
independent.model: Teacher paints the first pale wash on the orange, leaving its highlight.

independent.q: Extend: Evaluate your still life in the portal response box: two WWW and one EBI linked to the criteria. Start: 'What went well...'
independent.a: For example: WWW: overlap shows depth; tone follows the light. EBI: the bottle's ellipse could be more accurate.

independent.q: Stretch: Give a classmate's uploaded work one kind, specific comment in the portal.
independent.a: A comment naming one strength and one next step.

exit.q: In watercolour, highlights are made by... A) white paint B) leaving the paper white C) black paint
exit.a: B) leaving the paper white

exit.q: Big question: how do watercolour artists show the brightest highlights?
exit.a: By leaving the white paper unpainted.

lessons.homework: Photograph your finished still life in daylight and upload it to the portal for assessment with your evaluation.
lessons.send: SEND: a pre-drawn outline to paint. EAL: wash, water, dry, layer with gestures. Stretch: wet-in-wet background.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (Year 7 still life half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7
At home: three household objects (a mug, a fruit, a bottle), a desk lamp, sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, eraser
Watercolour set, round brush, two water pots, kitchen roll (pupil kit list)
Still life assessment rubric and evaluation frame (portal)

lessons.title: Drawing buildings from observation
lessons.bigQuestion: When you look out of your window, what makes a building look near or far?
objectives: To understand how to draw a building accurately using line, proportion and simple perspective
successCriteria: All: draw the main shapes of a building lightly
Most: measure proportions and add windows and doors accurately
Some: use one-point perspective to show depth

keywords.def: the front face of a building
the size of parts compared with each other
a way of showing depth on a flat page
where parallel lines seem to meet

hook.text: When you look out of your window, what makes a building look near or far?
hook.a: Size, detail and the way lines of roofs and windows slope towards the distance.

islamicLink.text: Muslim architects built with precision and beauty, from the Great Mosque of Cordoba to the Blue Mosque in Istanbul: careful looking and accurate measuring (itqan) came first.

starter.q: Value in art means ...
Name one watercolour technique from Spring 1.
A still life shows ...

teach.heading: Start with shapes
teach.note: Model a house front.

model.problem: Draw a street of buildings in one-point perspective
steps: Draw a horizon line
Mark one vanishing point
Draw the front faces as rectangles
Join corners to the vanishing point
Add windows that shrink towards it
model.answer: Buildings that recede into the distance

misconception.wrong: Windows all the same size along a receding wall
misconception.right: Windows get smaller and closer together towards the vanishing point

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: In one-point perspective, parallel lines going away from you ...
check.why: They converge at the vanishing point.

practice.q: Draw a box in one-point perspective.
practice.a: A rectangle front with corners joined to a vanishing point.
practice.model: I do: rectangle, dot on the horizon, lines from each corner to the dot, then the back edge.

independent.q: Draw a building from your window or a photo (no people): main shapes, proportions, details and one-point perspective if it fits.
independent.a: An accurate building drawing with details.
independent.model: The teacher draws the first stage on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add tone to show light on one side.
independent.a: Shaded side and lit side shown.

independent.q: Stretch: draw the same building from a second angle.
independent.a: A second viewpoint.

exit.q: A facade is ...
exit.a: the front face of a building
options: the front face of a building

exit.q: Back to our ponder: When you look out of your window, what makes a building look near or far?
exit.a: Size, detail and the way lines of roofs and windows slope towards the distance.

lessons.homework: Draw one more building detail (a door, window or roofline) from life.
lessons.send: SEND: chunked tasks, a key word glossary and sentence starters in the pupil PDF. EAL: key terms with definitions and examples. Stretch: evaluate, weigh up both sides and reach a justified judgement.
resources: Slides
Tarbiyyah Secondary Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 7 (buildings and Hundertwasser); Creative Arts five-year scheme (buildings topic only)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, HB and 2B pencils, ruler, fine black pen, watercolours or felt-tips, a window view or building photo
Photo of the finished work uploaded to the portal

lessons.title: Hundertwasser: colour, organic lines and buildings
lessons.bigQuestion: Hundertwasser said straight lines are not natural. Do you agree?
objectives: To understand how Friedensreich Hundertwasser used colour, organic lines and nature in his buildings
successCriteria: All: describe three features of Hundertwasser's buildings
Most: compare an organic line with a straight line
Some: explain his ideas about nature and buildings
lessons.smsc: Cultural: an artist who joined architecture and nature

keywords.def: flowing, natural shapes
Austrian artist and architect (1928 to 2000)
not regular or even
plants growing on a roof

hook.text: Hundertwasser said straight lines are not natural. Do you agree?
hook.a: Nature has few perfect straight lines; but straight lines are useful. Both have a place.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And the stars and trees prostrate.' (Ar-Rahman 55:6). Hundertwasser put trees on roofs and inside windows to bring nature into cities.

starter.q: A vanishing point is ...
Name one part of a facade.
Organic shapes are ...

teach.heading: Features
teach.note: Photos of Hundertwasserhaus (Vienna) and other buildings, without people.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

practice.q: Redraw a straight window as an organic, wavy window.
practice.a: A window with gently curved edges.
practice.model: I do: keep the size but wobble the edges like a leaf's outline.

independent.q: Sketchbook: draw a Hundertwasser-style facade study (no people): organic lines, varied windows, a roof garden.
independent.a: A facade study with three Hundertwasser features.
independent.model: The teacher sketches one wavy floor line.

independent.q: Extend: write two sentences comparing his style with a building near you.
independent.a: A reasoned comparison.

independent.q: Stretch: research one other Hundertwasser building and name it.
independent.a: For example: the Hundertwasser Toilets in Kawakawa, New Zealand.

exit.q: Hundertwasser was from ...
exit.a: Austria

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Hundertwasser said straight lines are not natural. Do you agree?
exit.a: Nature has few perfect straight lines; but straight lines are useful. Both have a place.
